stops.teaser: A bridge that was the longest in the world, built by the man who later did Brooklyn.

story: The bridge crosses the Ohio River between Cincinnati, Ohio, and Covington, Kentucky. It opened to traffic on January 1, 1867, with a main span of 1,057 feet. That made it the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time.

John A. Roebling designed it. The planning took years: Steamboat and ferry owners lobbied against the bridge, and the Ohio legislature refused a charter at first. The bridge was built almost entirely in Kentucky, because the state line follows the north bank of the river.

The tower foundations on the Covington side went smoothly. On the Cincinnati side, Roebling got stuck with water in the pit, so he designed his own wooden pumps from three-inch pine planks and built them in about forty-eight hours. His most famous design, the Brooklyn Bridge, opened in 1883.
stops.fact: He built his own pumps from pine planks.
stops.disputed: Many people say the Brooklyn Bridge came first. Wikipedia says the Cincinnati bridge opened in 1867, sixteen years before Brooklyn in 1883.

claims.t: The Roebling bridge opened on January 1, 1867.

claims.t: The bridge was finished after the Brooklyn Bridge.
claims.why: Brooklyn opened in 1883, sixteen years later.

story: The Tyler Davidson Fountain, also called The Genius of Water, was dedicated in 1871. It is the centerpiece of Fountain Square, at the corner of Fifth and Vine Streets, and the city's symbol.

The fountain is 43 feet tall and cast in bronze on a green granite base. The central figure, the Genius of Water, is nine feet high and weighs two tons. She pours water from hundreds of jets pierced in her outstretched fingers. The panels at the bottom show four uses of water: steam, water-power, navigation and the fisheries.

For more than 130 years it stood in the middle of Fifth Street. In 2006, during a renovation of the square, it was taken away and later put back in a wider space near the north end of the plaza, away from the traffic.
stops.disputed: Some people think it has always stood where it does today. Wikipedia says that for more than 130 years it stood in the middle of Fifth Street, and it was moved in the 2006 renovation.

story: Music Hall was completed in 1878. It was designed for two jobs: music in the central auditorium and industrial exhibitions in the side wings. It sits across from Washington Park in Over-the-Rhine.
The building is in the Venetian Gothic style, and it became a National Historic Landmark in January 1975. It is home to the Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra, the Pops, the Ballet and the Opera.

Springer Auditorium has a Czechoslovak chandelier that weighs about 1,500 pounds, is 21 feet wide and has 96 candles. After more than a year closed for a $143 million renovation, the hall reopened in 2017.
stops.disputed: Many people think a famous hall like this was built on empty land. Wikipedia says it was built over a pauper's cemetery.

claims.t: Music Hall is built in a plain, modern style.

story: The Carew Tower is a 49-story, 574-foot Art Deco skyscraper in downtown Cincinnati. It was the tallest building in the city from 1930 until 2011.

Industrialist John J. Emery wanted a "city within a city" with offices, shops, a hotel and a parking garage. It was announced shortly before the Great Depression began, but work kept going. The office tower topped out in July 1930, and the entire complex was done by early 1931 at a cost of $33 million.

The hotel opened as the St. Nicholas Plaza in 1931. The tower was named a National Historic Landmark in 1994. The National Park Service called it one of the finest examples of skyscraper modernism in America.
stops.fact: It was built during the Great Depression.
stops.disputed: Many people think the tower was built after the Depression. Wikipedia says work continued through the poor economy, with the tower topped out in July 1930.

claims.t: The Carew Tower was the tallest building in Cincinnati until 2011.
